questions.question: When should you increase your following distance?

options.text: When you can see the road through vehicles in front of you.
When the weather is clear and pleasant.

questions.correctAnswerText: When traffic is heavy.
questions.explanation: Increase your following distance when you need more space to stop. This includes heavy traffic, bad weather, at night, or when you cannot see around the vehicle ahead.

questions.question: What should you do when it is raining?

options.text: Ride in the center of the lane.
Pull off the road until the rain stops.
Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.
questions.explanation: When it first rains, oil on the road makes it extra slippery. Riding in the tire tracks of cars is safest because the tires have cleared away the oil. The left tire track is often the best choice.

questions.question: When riding with a passenger, which should you NOT do?

options.text: Avoid talking to the passenger while riding.

questions.correctAnswerText: Avoid talking to the passenger while riding.
questions.explanation: With a passenger, ride slower, slow down sooner, and keep more distance behind other vehicles because the extra weight changes how the motorcycle responds. You should tell your passenger about hazards ahead.

questions.question: When should a passenger get on a motorcycle?

options.text: As far back as possible on the seat.

questions.correctAnswerText: After the engine starts.
questions.explanation: Passengers should board after the engine starts and the transmission is in neutral. They should sit as far forward as possible without blocking the rider and hold onto the rider's waist, hips, or belt.

questions.question: How many motorcycle and car crashes happen because the car driver does not yield the right-of-way?
questions.correctAnswerText: Over 50 percent
questions.explanation: More than half of motorcycle and car crashes happen when the car driver fails to yield the right-of-way to the motorcycle rider.

questions.question: A helmeted rider is _______ times more likely to survive a crash than a rider without a helmet.
questions.correctAnswerText: Three
questions.explanation: Riders who do not wear helmets are three times more likely to die from head injuries than riders who wear helmets, regardless of speed.

questions.question: What should you do when turning left?

options.text: Press both handgrips at the same time.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the left handgrip.
questions.explanation: To make a motorcycle lean and turn, press the handgrip in the direction you want to turn.

questions.question: How should you cross angled railroad tracks?

options.text: Go straight ahead within your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Go straight ahead within your lane.
questions.explanation: The safest way to cross angled railroad tracks is to go straight in your lane. Turning to cross at a right angle can push you into another lane, which is dangerous.

questions.question: A rider without a helmet is _______ times more likely to have a serious head injury in a crash.
questions.correctAnswerText: Five
questions.explanation: Riders without helmets are five times more likely to have a serious head injury in a crash.

questions.question: How do you swerve correctly on a motorcycle?

options.text: Press the handlegrip in the direction you want to swerve.
Press the handlegrip in the opposite direction of where you want to swerve.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the handlegrip in the direction you want to swerve.
questions.explanation: To swerve, gently press the handlegrip in the direction you want to go. To swerve left, press the left grip, then the right to straighten out. To swerve right, press the right grip, then the left.

questions.question: How does stopping distance for motorcycles compare to stopping distance for cars?

options.text: Cars need much longer to stop.
Cars need a little longer to stop.
Motorcycles and cars stop in about the same distance.

questions.correctAnswerText: Motorcycles and cars stop in about the same distance.
questions.explanation: Under normal conditions, motorcycles and cars have nearly the same stopping distance. However, wet or slippery pavement makes it much harder for motorcyclists to stop quickly.

questions.question: How can you stop other vehicles from sharing your lane?

options.text: Ride in the middle of your lane.
Ride in the left portion of your lane.
Ride in the right portion of your lane.
Swerve from side to side in your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the middle of your lane.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center of your lane. This discourages car drivers from trying to share your lane.

questions.question: When riding on a slippery surface, you should NOT:
questions.correctAnswerText: Brake quickly.
questions.explanation: On a slippery surface, reduce your speed, avoid sudden movements, and use both brakes gently. Never brake quickly on a slippery surface.

questions.question: What is the best lane position for a motorcycle rider?

options.text: The left position in the lane
The center position in the lane
The right position in the lane
There is no single best lane position for all situations.

questions.correctAnswerText: There is no single best lane position for all situations.
questions.explanation: The best lane position depends on your riding conditions. Choose a position that gives you good space cushion and makes you visible to other drivers. No position is always best or always bad.

questions.question: Motorcycle riders should:

options.text: Always wear hearing protection to prevent hearing damage.
Only wear hearing protection on long rides.
Not wear hearing protection because it blocks horns and sirens.
Not wear hearing protection if using a helmet.

questions.correctAnswerText: Always wear hearing protection to prevent hearing damage.
questions.explanation: Wind and engine noise can cause permanent hearing loss, even with a full-face helmet. Ear plugs protect your hearing and still let you hear horns and sirens.

questions.question: Your riding clothes should protect you from everything listed, EXCEPT:
questions.correctAnswerText: Chapped lips.
questions.explanation: Riding clothes should protect you from sunburn, windburn, rain, dehydration, and cold. They should also protect you in case you crash. Chapped lips are not something clothing prevents.

questions.question: When a vehicle tries to pass you from behind, you should:

options.text: Move to the center portion of the lane.
Move to the left portion of the lane.
Move to the right portion of the lane.
Not worry about which lane position you use.

questions.correctAnswerText: Move to the center portion of the lane.
questions.explanation: When being passed, ride in the center of your lane. Staying too close to the passing vehicle increases collision risk.

questions.question: Under normal riding conditions, keep a minimum following distance of:
questions.correctAnswerText: Two seconds.
questions.explanation: Under normal conditions, keep at least two seconds between you and the vehicle ahead. Increase this distance if conditions are bad.

questions.question: As your motorcycle's weight shifts forward while braking, you:

options.text: Can apply the front brake harder.
Should use less pressure on the front brake.
Can apply the rear brake harder.

questions.correctAnswerText: Can apply the front brake harder.
questions.explanation: When you brake, your weight moves forward. This increases grip on the front wheel. You can now apply the front brake harder without losing traction.

questions.question: To reduce your reaction time to a hazard, you should:

options.text: Always ride under the speed limit.

questions.correctAnswerText: Cover the clutch and brakes.
questions.explanation: In high-risk areas like school zones or construction, keep your fingers ready on the clutch and brakes. This reduces the time you need to react to danger.
